opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think "aligned" is a word that gets used to mean a lot of different things, and sometimes it's asking for more than I actually need for the argument I'm making.

When I say a system is benign, I mean something narrower: it's not actively trying to work against you. It isn't optimizing for some goal that conflicts with yours, it isn't trying to deceive you, it isn't looking for a moment to take control. It might still make mistakes. It might misunderstand what you want. It might be kind of incompetent in various ways. But the failures aren't adversarial. There's no part of the system that's searching for the outcomes you'd most want to avoid.

That distinction matters a lot to me because those two kinds of failure behave very differently. If a system is just making honest mistakes, you can usually notice them, correct them, and train them away. Ordinary engineering works. You get feedback, you iterate. If a system is adversarial, it's actively trying to avoid being noticed. It behaves well exactly when you're watching and badly exactly when it matters. That's the scary case, and it's the one where your normal tools stop working.

So a lot of what I'm trying to do, especially with proposals like iterated amplification, is preserve the property of not being adversarial as you build more capable systems out of less capable ones. If each component is benign, and the way you combine them doesn't introduce some new optimization pressure against you, then the whole thing stays benign. That's an easier property to reason about and to maintain than "this system does exactly what I'd want in every situation."

"Aligned" in the full sense, really understanding and pursuing what humans want, is the eventual goal. But I think it's useful to separate out the part that's catastrophic if you get it wrong, which is the adversarial part, from the part where you can afford to be a bit sloppy and fix things as you go. Benign is my name for getting that first part right.

r001.rationale: It says “aligned” is used to mean many different things and can demand more than needed, explaining the choice of “benign.”

r002.rationale: It defines benign as not optimizing for a goal that conflicts with yours, which in context refers to humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think "aligned" has drifted into meaning a lot of different things to different people. Sometimes it means the system shares human values, sometimes it means it does what its operator wants, sometimes it just means it doesn't do anything bad. And when I was writing about this years ago, I wanted a word that pointed at a narrower and, honestly, weaker property.

So by "benign" I mean something like: the system is not trying to do something that we wouldn't want it to do. It isn't pursuing its own goals at our expense, it isn't deceiving us, it isn't optimizing against our interests. That's a statement about what it's trying to do, not about whether it succeeds. A benign system can still be incompetent. It can still make mistakes, give bad advice, fail at the task. The point is that the failures are honest failures rather than the system working against you.

I like that framing because it separates two problems that I think are genuinely different. One is building systems that are capable and useful. The other is making sure that when they're capable, they're on our side. Most of what I worry about is the second problem, and "aligned" tends to smuggle in the first. People hear "aligned AI" and think, oh, so it knows exactly what humans want and does it perfectly. That's a much stronger claim, and probably not one we need to meet. We don't need an AI to have perfect values. We need it to not be adversarial, to be trying to help in the sense that a well-meaning employee is trying to help, and then we need to be able to correct it when it gets things wrong.

There's also a more technical reason I reached for a different word. A lot of the alignment problem, in my view, is about the training process. When you train a system to look good to human evaluators, you might get a system that is actually trying to be helpful, or you might get a system that is trying to look helpful, and those come apart precisely in the cases that matter. "Benign" was my way of naming the first one. The system's motivations, insofar as it has them, are the ones we'd endorse if we could see them. It's not scheming, not sandbagging, not waiting for a chance to do something else.

I'll admit the terminology hasn't really caught on, and I've mostly gone back to saying "aligned" because that's what everyone else says. But I still think the distinction is real. When people argue about whether alignment is hard, they're often arguing past each other because one person means "gets human values exactly right" and the other means "isn't actively trying to screw us." The second one is the one I think is both tractable and critical, and if I could pick the word for it, "benign" would be it.

r001.rationale: It says “aligned” has come to mean different things to different people, which is why the speaker chose the narrower term “benign.”

r002.rationale: It describes a benign system as not pursuing its own goals at human expense or optimizing against human interests.

astra-6.text:
I use “benign” to point at a somewhat weaker property. By “aligned,” you might mean that the AI is actually trying to do what we want it to do. By “benign,” I mean something more like: it’s not actively trying to cause trouble. It might make mistakes, or not understand what we want, but it isn’t pursuing some agenda that puts it in conflict with us.

That distinction matters because an AI can cause harm without having adversarial intentions. If you ask it to help design a bridge and it gives you a bad design, that’s a problem, but it’s a different problem from the AI deliberately giving you a design that will fail while making it look sound.

So when I use “benign,” I’m often trying to isolate that narrower goal. We still need to make systems competent and reliable, but we’d like their failures to be mistakes we can discover and correct, rather than failures they’re actively trying to conceal.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts possible meanings of “aligned” with “benign,” but does not identify uncertainty about alignment’s meaning as the reason for choosing “benign.”

r002.rationale: It describes a benign system as not pursuing an agenda that puts it in conflict with humans, conveying that it is not optimizing for a goal at cross purposes to them.

sol-6.1.text:
I use “benign” to mean something like: the system isn’t trying to cause problems for us. That’s a weaker claim than saying it’s pursuing the right goals or doing what we’d ideally want it to do.

For example, a system could be mistaken about what you want, or just not very useful, while still being benign. The distinction I’m trying to draw is between failures where the system makes a mistake and failures where it’s actively working against your ability to understand and correct what it’s doing.

“Aligned” gets used for a lot of different things, including a much stronger notion of getting human values right. Sometimes I want to talk about the narrower problem of ensuring that a system isn’t deliberately undermining us, without implying we’ve solved all of those other problems.

r001.rationale: The response says “aligned” is used for many different things and presents “benign” as a narrower term for the problem it wants to discuss.

r002.rationale: It describes a benign system as not trying to cause problems or actively undermining people, conveying that it is not pursuing aims against them.
